descriptor: Partition, rearrange, regroup and rename two- and three-digit numbers using standard and non-standard groupings; recognise the role of a zero digit in place value notation.
scope: Year 2 core only. No invented next-year Stretch items: this website-bank build follows the agreed researched scope; app-specific adaptive/Stretch gates are not claimed.

teaching.title: Before you begin
teaching.unitKey: A hundred flat is worth 100. A ten rod is worth 10. A one cube is worth 1. H means hundreds, T means tens and O means ones.
notes: Partition means split a number into parts. Rearrange means move the whole parts into a different order. Keep each unit name with its number.
The usual grouping has fewer than 10 pieces in each place. Other equal groupings may have 10 or more tens or ones.
10 ones have the same value as 1 ten. 10 tens have the same value as 1 hundred. You can exchange in either direction.
Complete tens include the tens inside hundreds. Leftover ones are the ones left after making complete groups of ten.
A zero records an empty place in the usual numeral. No separate ten rods does not mean there are no tens inside the hundreds.
Use blocks, drawings or words for the tasks that ask you to show or explain. You may speak, sign or have someone write your explanation. These tasks wait for a grown-up’s check.

items.question: A class has 68 sticks. Write two different tens-and-ones names for all 68 sticks.
items.correct: For example, 6 tens and 8 ones; 5 tens and 18 ones. Both make 68.
items.explanation: Opening 1 ten gives 10 ones, so the total stays 68.
items.hint: The two names must have different numbers of tens.
items.misconception: Repeats the same grouping or changes the total during renaming.
items.modelAnswer: For example, 6 tens and 8 ones; 5 tens and 18 ones. Both make 68.
items.acceptanceNote: Accept any two distinct non-negative whole-number pairs (t,o) with 10t+o=68. Require unit labels. Reordering the same pair does not make a different grouping.

items.question: Which name has the same value as 2 hundreds, 3 tens and 8 ones?

items.hint: An extra ten must be worth 10, not 1.

items.question: Rename 615 using only complete tens and leftover ones.
items.explanation: 6 hundreds contain 60 tens. Add the other ten: 61 tens and 5 ones make 615.
items.hint: Include the tens inside the hundreds.

items.question: Sam says 451 = 4 hundreds + 5 tens + 1 one. Show a different equal name and explain why it still makes 451.

items.misconception: Gives a different-looking name without checking equal value.
items.acceptanceNote: Accept any equal, differently grouped non-negative whole-number name for 451 with a valid conserving explanation. Swapping digits does not meet the task. Spoken, signed, scribed or modelled reasoning is valid.

items.question: Complete both equal exchanges.
items.explanation: 10 ones and 1 ten have equal value. You can exchange in either direction.
items.hint: The unit changes; the total must stay the same.
items.misconception: Treats one ten as one one or loses loose ones during an exchange.

items.question: Complete both equal exchanges.
items.explanation: 10 tens make 100, so they equal 1 hundred. A hundred can be opened into 10 tens.
items.hint: A ten is worth 10; a hundred is worth 100.
items.misconception: Treats one hundred as one ten or omits existing hundreds/tens.

items.question: Open 1 ten in 76. Complete: 76 = 6 tens + ___ ones.
items.explanation: 7 tens become 6 tens and 10 ones. Join the 6 ones: 16 ones.
items.hint: Keep the original loose ones after the exchange.
items.misconception: Forgets the loose ones already present when opening a ten.

items.question: A model has 2 hundreds, 6 tens and 7 ones. Open 1 hundred into tens. How many tens will the new model have?
items.explanation: Opening 1 hundred gives 10 tens. The 6 tens already there remain: 16 tens.
items.hint: Add the new tens to the tens already there.
items.misconception: Counts only the new tens and omits existing tens.

items.question: Regroup 2 hundreds, 14 tens and 3 ones into the usual hundreds, tens and ones.
items.explanation: 14 tens are 1 hundred and 4 tens. With the 2 hundreds already there, the result is 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 3 ones.
items.hint: Each usual place has fewer than 10 pieces.
items.misconception: Concatenates a count greater than9 as if it were a single place digit.

items.question: Complete the equal name: 586 = 4 hundreds + ___ tens + 6 ones.
items.explanation: 586 = 400 + 180 + 6, so the missing count is 18 tens.
items.hint: Work with the value of the missing units.
items.misconception: Confuses the value of missing tens with the number of tens.

items.question: A model has 2 hundreds, 9 tens and 24 ones. Make every place have fewer than 10 pieces.
items.explanation: 24 ones become 2 tens and 4 ones. Now 11 tens become 1 hundred and 1 ten. The result is 3 hundreds, 1 ten and 4 ones.
items.hint: Regroup the ones, then check the tens again.
items.misconception: Stops after exchanging ones without checking the resulting tens.

items.question: There are 684 counters. Which trade keeps the total at 684?
items.explanation: Trading 1 hundred for 10 tens exchanges 100 for 100.
items.hint: Check the value of what leaves and what replaces it.
items.misconception: Trades pieces one for one despite unequal unit values.

items.question: Ella has 57 sticks. She renames them as 4 tens and 8 ones. Is her new name equal to 57? Explain, then fix it.
items.correct: No. 4 tens and 8 ones make 48. With 4 tens, she needs 17 ones to keep 57.
items.explanation: 57 = 5 tens and 7 ones = 4 tens and 17 ones.
items.hint: Check both totals before deciding whether a trade is equal.
items.misconception: Judges an exchange by appearance instead of comparing values.
items.modelAnswer: No. 4 tens and 8 ones make 48. With 4 tens, she needs 17 ones to keep 57.
items.acceptanceNote: Require recognition that 48 is not 57 and an equal correction, such as 4T17O or 5T7O. Accept any valid correction with total 57 and a value-based explanation. Do not award for only saying no.

items.question: A class packs 246 pencils. A box holds 100 and a bundle holds 10. There is 1 box, 14 bundles and 6 loose pencils. Make a new packing with fewer than 10 bundles. Explain your exchange.
items.correct: Exchange 10 bundles for 1 box. The new packing is 2 boxes, 4 bundles and 6 loose pencils, still 246.
items.explanation: 10 bundles of 10 equal one box of 100.
items.hint: Keep all the pencils while changing the packing.

items.modelAnswer: Exchange 10 bundles for 1 box. The new packing is 2 boxes, 4 bundles and 6 loose pencils, still 246.
items.acceptanceNote: Require a valid packing worth 246 with fewer than 10 bundles, including explanation of an equal exchange. 2 boxes/4 bundles/6 loose is the usual result. Accept other valid equal packings meeting the stated condition.

items.question: A model has 5 hundreds and 2 ones. Jo writes 52. Explain the mistake and write the correct numeral.
items.correct: Jo left out the empty tens place. 5 hundreds and 2 ones is 502. 52 means 5 tens and 2 ones.
items.explanation: The zero keeps the 5 in the hundreds place.
items.hint: Compare what the 5 is worth in each numeral.

items.modelAnswer: Jo left out the empty tens place. 5 hundreds and 2 ones is 502. 52 means 5 tens and 2 ones.
items.acceptanceNote: Require 502 and an explanation of the empty tens place or the change from 500 to 50 when zero is deleted. Accept spoken/modelled evidence; saying only add zero is insufficient.

items.question: Which sentence correctly names the tens in 400?
items.explanation: 400 = 40 tens. In the usual grouping of 4 hundreds, 0 tens and 0 ones, there are no separate ten rods.
items.hint: Distinguish the tens digit from all the complete tens inside the amount.
items.misconception: Treats the tens digit as the count of all complete tens.
answers: The tens digit is 0, and 400 contains 40 complete tens.
The tens digit is 0, so 400 contains no complete tens.
400 has 4 complete tens because its first digit is 4.

items.question: There are 600 paper squares. Write a different equal name that uses tens. Explain both zeros in 600.
items.correct: For example, 60 tens; or 5 hundreds and 10 tens. In the usual grouping, 600 has 0 separate tens and 0 loose ones.

items.modelAnswer: For example, 60 tens; or 5 hundreds and 10 tens. In the usual grouping, 600 has 0 separate tens and 0 loose ones.
items.acceptanceNote: Require an equal name with at least 1 ten and a correct explanation of zero tens/ones in usual notation. Accept any valid non-negative whole-number name totalling 600, such as 60T0O or 5H10T0O. Do not require the tens count to be a single digit.

items.question: Noah says 6 hundreds and 12 ones is the same as 5 hundreds and 12 tens. Is he correct? Explain using both totals.
items.correct: No. 6 hundreds and 12 ones is 612. 5 hundreds and 12 tens is 620. The totals are different.
items.explanation: 6 hundreds and 12 ones make 612. 5 hundreds and 12 tens make 620. The totals are different.

items.misconception: Ignores unit names when comparing the same written count.
items.modelAnswer: No. 6 hundreds and 12 ones is 612. 5 hundreds and 12 tens is 620. The totals are different.
items.acceptanceNote: Require no, both totals 612 and 620, and recognition that the names are unequal. Accept valid modelled or spoken evidence; no alone is insufficient.

items.question: Luca has 3 tens and 17 ones. Exchange 10 ones for 1 ten. Name the new grouping and explain why the amount stays the same.

items.modelAnswer: 4 tens and 7 ones. 10 ones and 1 ten both have value 10, so both groupings make 47.
items.acceptanceNote: Require 4T7O and valid explanation/evidence that 10 ones equal 1 ten, so the amount is conserved. Computing 47 is optional. Accept oral, scribed or constructed responses.

items.question: Regroup 2 hundreds, 7 tens and 34 ones into the usual grouping.

items.question: Tia has 3 tens and 15 ones. She trades 1 ten for 1 one and says she now has 2 tens and 16 ones. Is the trade equal? Repair it and explain why your new name keeps the same amount.
items.correct: No. The first grouping is 45; 2 tens and 16 ones is 36. Trading 1 ten gives 10 ones, so an equal result is 2 tens and 25 ones.
items.hint: Compare the value given away with the value received.
items.misconception: Judges an exchange by appearance instead of comparing values.
items.modelAnswer: No. The first grouping is 45; 2 tens and 16 ones is 36. Trading 1 ten gives 10 ones, so an equal result is 2 tens and 25 ones.
items.acceptanceNote: Require an unequal-trade judgement supported by values or model and a valid equal repair to 45. Accept 2T25O, 3T15O or 4T5O with a conserving explanation. Do not require one unique grouping.

items.modelAnswer: In 809, zero records no separate tens and keeps 8 in the hundreds place. 809 is 8 hundreds and 9 ones; 89 is 8 tens and 9 ones.
items.acceptanceNote: Require explanation of the empty tens place and differing hundreds/tens values. Accept equivalent spoken, signed, scribed or modelled reasoning.
